newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hebron deal held up, police remand second suspect.
newsitem.headline: Hebron deal held up, police remand second suspect.

text.p: Israeli police held a second soldier on Thursday in connection with the shooting of seven Arabs in Hebron as a deal with the PLO for Israel's redeployment in the West Bank town still eluded negotiators.

A top aide to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the PLO of stalling in the talks on Hebron but Palestinians said Israel's refusal to set dates for future redeployments was holding up an agreement.

U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross was meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in the Gaza Strip to nudge the two sides closer to a deal and agree to a summit but chances for a meeting between leaders later on Thursday appeared slim.
"Well, it's quite clear the stalling is being done by the Palestinian Authority," said Netanyahu's adviser David Bar-Illan just hours after predicting that a summit would be held on Thursday.
"The most reasonable guess is that they're doing it because they feel that the situation of no agreement favours them and is detrimental to us," he told Israel Radio.

Under a 1995 Israeli-PLO peace deal, 80 percent of Hebron was due to be handed over to Palestinians nine months ago. But violence, security concerns and other issues have held it up. Some 400 armed Jewish settlers live in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs.
Thursday's talks were conducted in the shadow of the wounding on Wednesday of seven Palestinians in Hebron by an off-duty Israeli soldier.
A magistrates court ordered Noam Friedman, an orthodox Jew from the West Bank settlement of Maaleh Adumim, held for 10 days on suspicion of murder and sedition.
The same court remanded the second suspect, Yuval Jibli, for four days after police arrested him late on Wednesday in connection with the shooting.
A police spokesman said Jibli was suspected of helping Friedman plan the attack in a crowded outdoor market in the West Bank town but the suspect told the court he was not involved.
Friedman, 22, told investigators he wanted to sabotage any transfer of power to Palestinians in Hebron.
Other soldiers jumped on Friedmen seconds after he began shooting his M-16 automatic rifle.
Israel Radio said Friedman told the court he regretted having failed to kill Palestinians in the attack. He protested against being remanded in a "secular court" by a woman judge, the radio said.
Netanyahu met on Thursday with the soldiers who overpowered Friedman and praised their actions.

"The actions of these people in the field, quick, daring, responsible actions...warrant commendation and admiration by Israel for the damage they prevented and the lives which were saved," said Netanyahu.

Palestinian negotiator Jamil al-Tarifi said the issue holding up an agreement was a PLO demand that Israel commit itself to target dates for further redeployments after Hebron, mostly in rural areas of the West Bank. These redeployments were already agreed in previous peace deals.

"Only one issue is left and after that a summit meeting will be set," chief Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas told Reuters after eight hours of talks with Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai that ended early on Thursday.
But Nabil Abu Rdainah, an adviser to Arafat, said: "Talks could drag on for a few more days."

The militant Islamic Jihad group meanwhile vowed in a leaflet to punish Israelis for the attack, describing the emerging deal on Hebron as "an agreement of shame" and saying the shooting would invite more atrocities against Palestinians.
